blocks.heading: Organisational structure
blocks.text: An organisational structure is the levels of management and divisions of responsibilities within an organisation. It clarifies who performs each role, who may decide and who reports to whom. This can reduce duplicated work and gaps where everyone assumes someone else is responsible. In a centralised structure most decisions are retained at the centre or higher management levels. In a decentralised structure many decisions are delegated to lower levels. The distinction concerns the location of decision-making authority, not the number of buildings or whether the business uses computers. A structure can combine central financial policy with decentralised local service decisions. Clear roles help accountability, but the chart alone cannot ensure cooperation or competent decisions. Structure should fit the scale, activities and skills of the enterprise.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Huma Stores has three branches. Head office sets the purchasing budget while branch managers may arrange their staff rotas. Purchasing authority is centralised while rota decisions are decentralised. Three locations do not by themselves prove decentralisation; identify the decision and the person authorised to make it.

blocks.heading: A centralised structure
blocks.text: A centralised structure is a management structure in which most decisions are taken at the centre, or at higher levels of management. It can support consistent policy and senior oversight, especially where decisions carry substantial risk. However, referring routine matters upward can delay a response and overload senior managers. The location of offices is not the test; locate the authority.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: All Iita Stores branches must ask head office before changing product prices. Pricing is centralised even though branches are geographically separate. The branches carry out the decisions but do not make them.

blocks.heading: A decentralised structure
blocks.text: A decentralised structure is a management structure in which many decisions are not taken at the centre of the business but are delegated to lower levels of management. It can use local knowledge and reduce waiting for head-office approval. Its effectiveness depends on staff competence, clear limits and coordination; different decisions can otherwise become inconsistent. Senior managers retain overall oversight.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Meva Lodges allows each lodge manager to choose locally suitable guest activities within a budget. The activity decisions are decentralised. A shared budget policy does not remove the local authority that has been granted.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain why saying “three levels of managers” is not a complete definition of organisational structure. Otavi Makers also needs to know which roles handle production, finance and sales.

Hierarchy describes ranked levels. Organisational structure includes levels and the division of responsibilities, so the three-level statement omits who does what and reports to whom. Allocating production, finance and sales roles supplies part of the missing structure; counting levels alone cannot do that.
